newsitem.title: CANADA: Irish guerrilla deported from Canada, fears for life.
newsitem.headline: Irish guerrilla deported from Canada, fears for life.

text.p: A former Northern Ireland guerrilla who feared retribution by his one-time comrades was set to be deported to Britain on Wednesday after losing a long legal battle to stay in Canada.

A lawyer for Patrick Ward said the former high-ranking officer in the Irish National Liberation Army (INLA) faced a death threat by the group, but would be put on a flight to London after a deportation order on Tuesday by a Canadian court. "He has a genuine fear. There is a death threat
issued against him (by the INLA)," Ward's lawyer Irvin Sherman told Reuters. "He's leaving with a great deal of reluctance."
Sherman said that under Britain's Prevention of Terrorism Act, Ward could be ordered out of Britain to Northern Ireland within the next three years.
A federal judge on Tuesday rejected Ward's application to stay in Canada, saying there was not enough evidence to justify his fears of retaliation, since most of his enemies had been killed.

Sherman said the death threat followed an incident in 1983 when the INLA, a shadowy leftish Republican group considered more extreme than the Irish Republican Army, ordered Ward to kill a man and child the group was holding captive.
Ward refused and let them escape, his lawyer said.

Afterward, the INLA kidnapped Ward's wife and two daughters -- who still live in Northern Ireland -- to prevent Ward from giving evidence against the group, and tortured him. Ward's family was released when he was charged by authorities.
Ward pleaded guilty to forcible confinement and served three years in prison before coming to Canada in 1985.
He was ordered deported a year later. In 1988, he was granted refugee status in Canada, which was revoked in 1990.
The Supreme Court of Canada later sent Ward's case to the refugee board, which ruled he was not a refugee.
The INLA, which broke away from the IRA 25 years ago, seeks an end to British rule in Northern Ireland and bitterly opposed the IRA's decision to declare a cease-fire in August 1994.
The group's decision not to participate in the truce led to an internal feud in which three people, including a nine-year-old girl, were killed last year.
In 1979, the INLA killed British MP Airey Neave, a close adviser of Margaret Thatcher before she became British prime minister.
